Scaling Up Platform · Progress Update · July 2, 2026

Your clients' assessment history now comes with them

Yesterday's update showed "bringing your history over" as the item being built. Today it is live on the platform — a coach can import a company's past Scaling Up Full assessment rounds out of Esperto and get real, scored reports plus the year-over-year comparison. This update covers exactly what shipped in the last two days, how it was proven safe, and what's next. Real screens throughout, captured today on the live platform.

What's new — and what it looks like

One headline feature this time, taken from idea to live in 48 hours — with an unusual amount of proof behind it.

Yesterday, this screen was a roadmap item. The import tool could bring in people (rosters) and one assessment type's past answers — and the July 1 update listed historical Scaling Up Full import as the thing being built next.
Today, it's live. LIVE The same screen on the production platform this morning: a third option — SU-Full (historical) — with a plain-language flow: name the round (e.g. "2025 Annual", "Year 1"), pick which company it belongs to, and upload the export files for that round. The header copy updates itself too: "Supported today: Members rosters, QSP-v2 results, and Scaling Up Full (historical results)."

How a coach uses it, start to finish:

  • 1. Import the company's roster first (same as before) — that's how historical answers get matched to real people.
  • 2. Pick "SU-Full (historical)", name the round, choose the company, and upload the round's export files from Esperto.
  • 3. Preview. Nothing is written yet — the platform shows exactly what it will import, who resolved, and anything it will skip, before you commit.
  • 4. Commit. The round lands as a closed, back-dated campaign: real per-person reports, scored by our engine — and it never emails anyone.
Why history matters: every imported round feeds this — the year-over-year comparison that launched June 30. Import "Year 1" and "Year 2" from Esperto, and a client's progress story is on one screen the day they join the platform.

What protects a client's history (all live, all exercised on production):

  • Re-uploading the same round twice does nothing — the platform recognizes identical data and refuses to create duplicates.
  • Uploading changed data under the same round name is refused with a clear error — history is never silently rewritten.
  • Wrong files are refused cleanly at the door (we verified this by accident, with a wrongly-shaped file of our own — it was turned away exactly as designed).
  • Every import is tied to one named company you choose explicitly — the platform never guesses which company a file belongs to.

Proven against Esperto itself — not assumed

This is the part that took the time, and it's the reason the feature can be trusted with real client history.

Esperto's export files carry answers under code names like Q7_3 — with no question text at all. And it turned out the codes are not in the order the survey shows them. Guess the mapping wrong, and every imported report silently attaches answers to the wrong questions — the numbers still look plausible, so nobody would ever notice. Two sections were genuinely indistinguishable by any file we had:

Scalability & Technology
6 questions
⇄
Internal Communication
6 questions
A positional guess would have swapped these two sections in every imported report — invisibly. Four more 5-question sections had the same ambiguity among themselves.

So we didn't guess — we asked Esperto. We ran controlled test submissions into the real Esperto tool: filled section 1 entirely with 1s, section 2 with 2s, and so on — then read the export back. Whichever code family came back as all-5s is section 5. A second run with a different value on every single row confirmed the order of questions inside each section too. Every mapping in the shipped feature traces to that experiment, not to an assumption. (All Esperto-side test data was deleted afterwards; the account was left exactly as found.)

Then we proved the whole pipeline end-to-end with a known-answer test on production. Because we planted the values ourselves, the correct report was known in advance — and the live platform reproduced it exactly:

SectionValues we plantedReport must showReport showed

Company Culture1,2,3,4,5avg 3.0 · 15 pts3.0 · 15 ✓
Strategy1…7avg 4.0 · 28 pts4.0 · 28 ✓

All 63 imported answers (61 sliders + the two team-size fields) matched position-for-position; the report totals (231 points, 3.79 average) matched the arithmetic exactly. The test round was then removed from production using the same removal tool we'd reach for in a real incident — which means the emergency path has now been rehearsed for real, too.

The launch was run like a fire drill — and the drill caught three real things

Staged rollout, each step gated on evidence. The catches below were found by the process itself and fixed the same day, before any coach could hit them.

0 · VerifyControlled Esperto submission proves every mapping
PASSED
1 · PilotKnown-answer import into a test company on production data
PASSED
2 · CanaryFeature armed for the one test company only; duplicate + tamper defenses exercised live
PASSED
3 · Go liveSwitched on for everyone; live checks on coach + admin screens
LIVE
4 · Clean upTest round surgically removed — rollback tooling rehearsed on production
PASSED
Caught by the pre-launch check — before any import could fail

1 · The live questionnaire had quietly gained a required question

The current live version of the Scaling Up Full questionnaire includes a required team-size question that the import mapping (written against the earlier version) didn't carry. Left alone, every single import would have been skipped as "incomplete" — the feature would have shipped broken. The pre-launch check caught it; the mapping was extended (the team-size fields were already verified in the Esperto experiment) and, as a bonus, imported reports now carry growth-phase data.

Caught by the pilot — fixed for all future large imports

2 · The database time budget was too tight for big batches

The import's save step ran under a 5-second internal time limit — fine for small tests, but uncomfortably tight for a full leadership-team round (and it's rated for up to 300 files). The pilot tripped it; the budget is now 55 seconds. Every failed attempt rolled back cleanly to nothing — the all-or-nothing design held under real failure.

Caught by the go-live check — fixed within the hour

3 · The page still said the feature didn't exist

With the feature switched on, the import page offered SU-Full — while its own header still read "Supported today: Members rosters and QSP-v2 results." The sentence now updates itself with the feature switch (and reads correctly in both states).

Honest footnote: monitoring for this feature is currently a human reading structured production logs (every import attempt, refusal, and conflict is logged in detail) plus an instant kill switch — automated alerting is on the hardening list below, sized for when import traffic actually grows.

Rockefeller + LVA history import

Needs one thing from you

The import machinery built for Scaling Up Full — the staging, the duplicate/tamper defenses, the company matching — is generic. Each remaining assessment type only needs its own verified question mapping, and the Esperto-experiment method above makes that a short, repeatable job.

  • Blocked on: real Rockefeller and LVA export files (and Esperto access to run the same verification experiment against those questionnaires).
  • Until then, the platform deliberately refuses Rockefeller/LVA history uploads rather than guessing — the same no-silent-corruption rule that governed SU-Full.
2

Quick fixes from the July 1 list

Small · buildable now

Each of these was checked against the actual code before landing here — two turned out to be different (and easier) than they first appeared.

  • The "duplicate" QSP question isn't a stray copy — investigation: the survey deliberately carries three identically-labeled "share the stories" slots, ported faithfully from Esperto. The fix is differentiating the labels ("Story 1 / 2 / 3"), not deleting a question — no answers are lost.
  • Coach completion email says "a responder" instead of the person's name — investigation: the email does insert a name when the respondent record has one; the generic wording is a missing-name fallback. Fix: fall back to the person's roster name, then their email — never a generic word.
  • "Leadership Team" label capitalization — one-line wording fix in the LVA survey.
  • Core-values question rewording — the suggested copy is already in hand ("What are your core values? If not yet set, what do you think the top 3 should be?").
  • Possible duplicate: "most important thing to achieve this year's goals" — we'll verify against the adjacent question and the Esperto source before touching it (same no-guessing rule as the import work).
